paras: The Beaumont refinery notices were threats posted in May 1903 at the oil refineries in the South End of Beaumont, Texas, ordering Black workers to leave under threat of death. No attack, arrest or departure of workers was reported in the coverage found. The episode drew comment mainly in the Black press, where a Dallas Express editorial reprinted by the Colored American treated the notices as the work of "whitecaps" trying to drive Black men from their jobs.
Black men were working in the Beaumont oil refineries at the time, according to the Dallas Express, which wrote of "the colored men who are now employed" there.

According to a Beaumont dispatch printed in the St. Landry Clarion of Opelousas, Louisiana, on 9 May 1903, men going to work at the South End refineries "yesterday morning" found a notice posted there. It stated that "the negroes must leave the place at once" or face what the printed text rendered as "(skull and bones)," with the line "You know what that means" beneath. The dispatch named no author and gave no count of the workers concerned.

The Dallas Express gave a somewhat different version, speaking of notices in the plural and attributing them to "whitecaps." In its account the warning was addressed to the oil refiners, who "must not employ colored men," rather than to the workers themselves.

No report of arrests, an investigation, or Black workers leaving the refineries appears in the coverage. The Dallas Express wrote that Black people who appealed to officers in such "whitcap affairs" as a rule got "no relief."

The only white-press report found is a one-paragraph brief headed "Negroes Threatened," run in a column of short Louisiana and Texas items that also covered the New Orleans screwmen's strike. It quoted the notice's threat and offered no comment.

The Black press, by contrast, read the notices as part of a wider pattern. On 16 May 1903 the Colored American reprinted "verbatim" a Dallas Express editorial it called "editorial wisdom," which argued that the same whitecaps would have run Black men out as vagrants had they refused work, and would have ordered Black farmers off their land "on pain of death." The editorial held that the "proscribed laborer" could not solve the problem alone and urged "the better element of white people" to "take a hand in silencing these whitecap creatures."

reader.title: Beaumont refinery notices
bases: A posted notice threatened Black refinery workers with death if they did not leave (A1), and the Dallas Express said the notices warned refiners not to employ colored men (A3); no attack, expulsion carried out, or action by white workers is reported (A1, A3, A4).

A Beaumont wire brief in a white paper (A1) and a Dallas Express editorial reprinted in the Black press (A3) both report threatening notices posted at the Beaumont refineries against Black workers; the Express adds details (the 'whitecaps' label, the demand on employers) absent from A1, suggesting it did not simply copy that brief.

accounts.label: Beaumont wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Men going to work at the South End refineries found a notice that the negroes must leave the place at once or face '(skull and bones)', with 'You know what that means' below.

accounts.label: Dallas Express editorial (reprinted by the Colored American)
accounts.gist: Whitecaps posted notices at Beaumont warning the oil refiners not to employ colored men; Black appeals to officers in such affairs bring no relief, and white people of the 'better element' must act.

framing.detail: A short dispatch headed 'Negroes Threatened' in a column of Louisiana and Texas news items, quoting the notice without comment.
The Colored American reprinted as 'editorial wisdom' a Dallas Express piece calling the posters 'whitecap creatures' and faulting the 'lax and lame arm of the law'.

versions.value: The negroes must leave the place at once
The oil refiners must not employ colored men

conflicts.note: Different emphasis rather than contradiction: the wire brief addressed the notice to Black workers, the Dallas Express to their employers; both may describe the same notices.
